title: Why Avoidance Is A Terrible Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In this pointed critique, Michael Linsin takes aim at a common but misguided response to misbehavior: broadly restricting student freedoms rather than addressing the underlying conduct itself. He gives examples such as separating students who don't get along or banning materials like clay because they were misused, arguing that these blanket restrictions punish students unnecessarily and strip them of chances to grow. Linsin contends the real solution is to teach expectations in detail, model desired behavior, and hold students accountable to clear rules and consequences rather than removing the opportunity for misbehavior altogether. He frames this as essential to helping students develop self-control, responsibility, and the ability to work with people and situations they don't naturally handle well. The article closes with a call to outlaw the misbehavior itself rather than the activities and freedoms surrounding it, positioning this as central to building mature, capable students.
points: Avoidance strategies — separating students, banning materials or activities because of past misbehavior — punish the whole group and signal that students can't improve.
These broad restrictions limit students' social and academic development and rob them of creativity and joy.
The alternative is to teach expectations in detail, model behavior for every activity and transition, and hold students accountable through clear rules and consequences.
Systematically removing challenging people, activities, or situations makes students less mature, tolerant, empathetic, and self-controlled over time.
The goal should be to outlaw the actual misbehavior itself, not the freedoms and opportunities that make misbehavior possible.
quotes: It’s avoidance. It’s limiting the healthy freedoms of students in order to avoid the possibility that misbehavior could occur.

Not to be confused with the effective use of consequences, these broad reactions punish students unnecessarily and send the message that they don't have the capacity to improve or do things the right way.
The alternative is to teach students in detail what your expectations are. Model for them, show them, how to behave during every activity, transition, task, and routine throughout the school day.
When we systematically and arbitrarily remove people, things, situations, and ideas they don’t naturally handle well, or may not like or agree with, we do them a disservice.
So instead of trying to avoid misbehavior by limiting the very things that help your students grow into responsible adults, outlaw the actual misbehavior itself.
We teach them patience, kindness, understanding, appreciation, self-restraint, discipline, discernment, and the tools to handle themselves with grace and aplomb.
